newsitem.title: USA: KeyCorp's strategy faces revenue challenge.
newsitem.headline: KeyCorp's strategy faces revenue challenge.

text.p: KeyCorp, the $65 billion asset bank holding company based in Cleveland, faces challenges in its strategy to be a nationwide financial services company.

"We think the greater risk is on the revenue side," said analyst Sandra Flannigan of Merrill Lynch & Co. She said the company will have to keep revenue growth going while engaged in a downsizing of their branch banking system.
"We aim to be a national provider (of financial services)," said Bill Murschel, a KeyCorp spokesman. He said parts of Key are already a nationwide company.
Murschel said the company's KeyBank USA consumer finance unit already competes in most of the U.S., doing business beyond the 14 states where it operates through 12 charters.

KeyBank USA is involved in such areas as credit cards, educational loans and prime and sub-prime auto lending. Murschel said the company wants to have a national brand similar to that of McDonald's Corp and Sears Roebuck & Co.
Murschel said all of Key's banks will be converted to national charters next year and later they will be rolled into one national charter.

The ratings agency Standard & Poor's noted that since the 1994 merger of Albany, N.Y.-based Key and Cleveland-based Society Corp, the company has experienced "lackluster revenue dynamics" despite its retail presence in the fairly strong Midwest and Rocky Mountain regions.

S&P said KeyCorp has been bolstering profitabilty through recognition of gains on sales of assets via securitizations, and other non-recurring items. S&P, noting that Key will take a $100 million restructuring charge in the fourth quarter, reaffirmed its A-2 commercial paper rating and ratings of A-minus on senior debt and BBB-plus on subordinated debt.

Several analysts noted that announcement of a plan to repurchase up to 12 million shares through the end of 1997 helped push the stock of KeyCorp higher. The company had 227.6 million shares outstanding at the end of September.

Analyst Kevin Timmons of First Albany Co, noting plans to sell some branches and consolidate others, said, "the banking business is in the process of moving from physicial delivery of services at branches to electronic delivery."

Flannigan of Merrill Lynch said while there will always be a need for a branch system there is also a need for alternate channels to meet the changing needs of customers. The analyst said she remains neutral on the stock.
